strengths: First work (to the authors' knowledge) to bring the datamodels/data attribution framework to robot imitation learning, addressing genuine obstacles (expensive rollouts, non-differentiable success metrics, noisy per-sample influence) with sensible adaptations such as the differentiable validation-loss proxy metric and cluster-level influence estimation.

Empirically validates the key design choice: Figure 2 shows that the rollout-based metric M can be replaced by the proxy metric with only marginal performance loss, and that the metagradient estimator is ~8x faster with a small drop, making the method practical at scale.

Comprehensive evaluation breadth: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 tasks with Octo, and four real-world tasks drawn from heterogeneous OXE subsets, including the challenging cross-embodiment (Tiago-Sink) and multitask (Droid-Multitask) settings.

Consistent gains over reasonable similarity-based baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR) plus Target-Only and All-Data/Random controls; ~10% boost over SOTA on MetaWorld and clearly strongest real-world average (61.0 vs ~40 for baselines).

Good qualitative analysis (what data is selected, distribution over source datasets, top/bottom ranked samples) that builds intuition for why performance-aware selection beats similarity heuristics, and an honest limitations section.
Method is technology-agnostic (works with MLP policies and transformer diffusion policies like Octo), suggesting broad applicability within robot learning.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the core machinery (linear datamodels, regression estimator, metagradient/MAGIC influence estimation) is adopted from prior NLP/CV work [22, 24, 45]; the contribution is primarily an application plus engineering adaptations (proxy metric, clustering, target-data mixing) rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Statistical rigor is thin in the most impactful experiments: all real-world evaluations were run with a single random seed, and LIBERO uses 5 seeds but margins are small (DataMIL 37.76 vs STRAP 34.96 vs Flow 35.42), with DataMIL losing outright to baselines on several tasks (e.g., Stove-Moka, Bowl-Cabinet, Mug-Mug, Mug-Pudding).

The proxy metric is validated on only a single MetaWorld task (pick-place-wall); no evidence is given that validation-loss correlation with true success holds for the larger Octo policies or the real-world settings where the proxy is actually used.

Reported compute cost is a significant practical concern: datamodel estimation is 'several times the cost of training on all the data,' and the paper provides little quantitative cost accounting per setting (only an 8x relative speedup claim for metagradients vs. regression).

Ad hoc hyperparameters weaken the 'end-to-end, assumption-free' narrative: hand-tuned pre-grasp state weighting (w=2), per-task selection budgets, clustering granularities chosen per dataset, and co-training ratio alpha=0.5, with limited ablation of these choices.

MetaWorld experiments use a relatively simple state-based MLP policy, which is the easiest regime for influence estimation; the harder, more representative image-based settings (LIBERO, OXE) show narrower gains.
Differences from published STRAP numbers are explained only qualitatively (evaluation protocol, policy architecture); a direct apples-to-apples replication would have strengthened credibility.

Reproducibility details for the metagradient-based estimator in the robotics setting are deferred to external references [24, 45], and no code release is mentioned in the main text (only a website link).

strengths: First application of the datamodels/data attribution framework to robot imitation learning, addressing a genuine and timely problem (selecting task-relevant subsets of large prior datasets like OXE for post-training)

Substantial experimental scope: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO tasks, and real-world evaluations on four OXE settings including a cross-embodiment (Tiago) and multitask scenario, with several relevant baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR, SR)

Reasonable practical adaptations for robotics: rollout-free differentiable proxy metric, cluster-level (sub-trajectory) influence estimation to reduce noise, and inclusion of target data during datamodel estimation to mitigate distribution shift

Transparent reporting: detailed baseline implementation notes, discussion of discrepancies with the original STRAP paper, qualitative analyses of selected data, and a candid limitations section (compute cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, target-task scale)
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core machinery (regression datamodels, metagradient estimators, validation-loss-based proxy) is directly borrowed from prior work [22, 24, 45]; the robotics contribution is largely an assembly of existing estimators plus engineering fixes rather than a new technique

The proxy metric is simply negative behavior-cloning loss on held-out target data, so the paper's central 'novel surrogate loss' claim is overstated; this is a standard validation-loss proxy and the evidence for its correlation with true success is a single MetaWorld task (Fig. 2), with DataMIL-meta visibly lower than DM-rollouts

High cost undercuts the value proposition: even with metagradients, datamodel estimation costs several times training on all data, and the regression estimator requires thousands of policy trainings plus rollouts, limiting practical adoption

Simulation gains over the strongest baselines are modest and often within error bars: on LIBERO-10 DataMIL averages 37.76% vs. Flow's 35.42% and STRAP's 34.96%, and DataMIL is not best on all tasks (e.g., Stove-Moka, Bowl-Cabinet); the 10% MetaWorld improvement is the main sim result

Real-world evaluations are thin: 10-39 rollouts per task, all conducted with a single random seed, and datamodel-estimation choices (selection ratio, clustering granularity, state re-weighting w(s,a)=2 for pre-grasp states) appear tuned per setting without ablation or justification, raising concerns about generalization of the recipe

No ablations on key design choices (clustering scale, fraction of target data mixed in during datamodel estimation, selection budget x%, co-training ratio alpha), and no comparison to recent related curation methods such as Re-Mix or mutual-information-based curation

Hyperparameters and target-task-scale limitations, while acknowledged, are significant: the method is currently restricted to single-task (or tiny multitask) targets, which is precisely the regime where the practical payoff is least clear

strengths: Novel and meaningful contribution: to the authors' knowledge (and the reviewer's), this is the first work to bring the datamodels/data-attribution framework to robot imitation learning, addressing the unique obstacles (expensive/non-differentiable rollouts, per-example influence noise, severe distribution shift) in a principled way.

The rollout-free, differentiable proxy metric (behavior-cloning loss on held-out target data, Eq. 4) is a sensible and well-motivated solution that makes both regression and metagradient estimators usable in robotics; the ablation comparing DM-rollouts vs DataMIL-rg vs DataMIL-meta (Fig. 2) directly validates this design choice.

Broad and relevant experimental scope: 50 MetaWorld tasks, LIBERO-10 with a real foundation policy (Octo), and real-world selection from heterogeneous OXE datasets, including the hard cross-embodiment (Tiago) and multitask (Droid) settings—covering exactly the regimes where heuristic selection is claimed to break down.

Strong baselines from recent literature (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR/SR, Random, Target-Only, All-Data) with documented effort to give baselines fair budgets and tuned variants (e.g., horizon-based similarity for MetaWorld, matched selection budget for STRAP), which strengthens the credibility of the comparisons.

Helpful qualitative analyses (composition of selected datasets, top/bottom ranked samples in Fig. 5-7, Fig. 8) that give insight into why performance-aware selection works where similarity heuristics fail.
Honest limitations section (compute cost, hyperparameters, target-task scale) and transparent discussion of discrepancies with original STRAP numbers.
weaknesses: Real-world evaluation rigor is limited: all OXE results use a single random seed and modest numbers of rollouts (14-39 evaluations per task, e.g., 17 poses for Franka-Pouch), with no confidence intervals. Several headline real-world gains (e.g., 70.6 vs 41.2 for Franka-Pouch) could partly reflect evaluation noise; real-world real-averages (61.0 vs ~40) would be more convincing with seed variance.

Simulation margins are mixed: the LIBERO improvement is modest (37.76 vs 34.96 STRAP, 36.4 BR), and DataMIL underperforms baselines on several tasks (Bowl-Cabinet, Stove-Moka, and a near-total failure on Mug-Mug at 0.8). The claim of 'consistent gains' is somewhat stronger than the per-task evidence.

The core technical machinery (datamodels, regression estimator, metagradient estimator) is adopted from prior work [22, 24, 45]; the contribution is primarily an adaptation (proxy metric, clustering, target-data mixing, co-training recipe). This is valuable but somewhat incremental on the methods side.

Evidence that the proxy metric correlates with true success is shown on a single task (pick-place-wall in MetaWorld); a broader correlation analysis across tasks/policy classes would substantiate the central assumption more convincingly.

Several hyperparameters appear tuned per benchmark (sub-trajectory horizon 15 for LIBERO, pre-grasp state weighting w(s,a)=2 for LIBERO, trajectory-level clustering for OXE, alpha=0.5, per-task selection ratios), which raises concerns about generalization of the recipe to new settings and the risk of evaluation-set tuning; no sensitivity analysis is provided.

Practicality concerns: the authors acknowledge datamodel estimation costs several times the cost of training on all data, which undercuts the efficiency argument relative to simply co-training on the full prior dataset, particularly for large policies.

Some presentation issues: 'SR' baseline appears in the MetaWorld discussion and Figure 8 but is not clearly introduced in the main-text baseline list; minor inconsistencies (e.g., 'DaMIL' in Figure 1, section numbering references).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem—performance-aware data selection for robot imitation learning—and provides a well-motivated framing of why heuristic similarity-based selection is insufficient.

The proposed adaptations of datamodels to robotics are sensible and practically significant: a differentiable, rollout-free proxy metric (held-out BC loss), cluster-level influence estimation, and a distribution-shift mitigation strategy that includes target data during datamodel estimation.

The evaluation is broad and convincing: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 long-horizon tasks, and real-robot experiments on OXE, including a challenging cross-embodiment setting (Tiago) and a multitask setting (Droid), with consistent gains over strong baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR/SR).
Good ablation coverage: selection ratio, cluster size, co-training ratio, extended training for the All-Data baseline, and no-goal-conditioning experiments in the appendix.

Validation of the core proxy metric against true rollout success (Fig. 2, App. C.1), qualitative analysis of what data is selected, and an unusually honest limitations section including compute costs (3-4 days on 4xA100 for OXE selection).
Reproducibility appears good: pseudocode for both estimators, detailed hyperparameter tables, dataset composition tables, and released code/website.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: the core machinery (linear datamodels, regression estimator, metagradient/MGD estimator) is taken directly from prior work (Ilyas et al. 2022; Engstrom et al. 2025); the contribution is largely an application with engineering adaptations, and the paper sits close to concurrent work (CUPID).

The central assumption—that held-out BC loss is a good surrogate for true task success—is validated only on one main task plus four appendix tasks; a more systematic correlation analysis across diverse tasks would strengthen the claim, especially since the authors themselves note validation loss is a noisy predictor in robotics.

Real-world results are statistically fragile: single seed, small numbers of rollouts per task (10-39), and some gains over the best baselines are modest (e.g., LIBERO average 37.76 vs. 36.4 for BR; several LIBERO tasks where STRAP or BR outperform DataMIL).

Evidence of per-method tuning that could favor DataMIL: e.g., the pre-grasp state up-weighting (w=2) used only in LIBERO, and task-specific selection ratios (1%, 0.75%, 0.5%); the baselines may not have received equivalent care despite the fair-comparison efforts described in App. E.

Scalability of the method is a real concern the authors acknowledge: the metagradient estimator is 3-5x slower than standard policy training and requires days of GPU time on large corpora, weakening the practicality argument versus cheap similarity-based retrieval.

The MetaWorld regression estimator requires 10^4 policy trainings; while amortized across 50 tasks, this design is only feasible in the simplest setting, so the strongest gains are obtained with the most expensive estimator.
Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'effect' vs 'affect', inconsistent metric naming Mc/M-wide-hat), and Table 1 reveals mixed per-task results that the average somewhat obscures.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and timely problem: performance-aware data selection for robot imitation learning, moving beyond heuristic similarity-based curation to a framework that directly estimates each datapoint's influence on downstream task success.

The proposed adaptations of datamodels to robotics are sensible and well-motivated: a differentiable BC-loss proxy metric that removes the need for expensive real-world rollouts, cluster-level (trajectory/sub-trajectory) influence estimation to reduce noise, and mixing target data during datamodel estimation to mitigate distribution shift.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad and thorough: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 tasks with Octo, and real-robot experiments on four tasks across three embodiments (including a cross-embodiment setting where the target robot never appears in the prior data), with reasonable baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR) and multiple ablations (selection ratio, cluster size, co-training ratio, extended training for the All-Data baseline).

The analysis of what data is selected (Figs. 5-7, App. A) provides useful qualitative insight, e.g., that harmful data often looks visually similar to helpful data, and that DataMIL selects more balanced dataset mixtures than baselines.
Limitations are candidly acknowledged in the conclusion, and the appendix provides substantial detail on hyperparameters, computation costs, and discrepancies with previously reported STRAP numbers.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited: the framework is a fairly direct combination of existing techniques (linear datamodels from Ilyas et al., exact metagradients from Engstrom et al./MAGIC) with a straightforward proxy metric (negative BC loss on a held-out target set). The core methodological contribution is adaptation/engineering rather than a new idea, which may be viewed as incremental for a top-tier AI conference.

The computational cost is significant: the regression estimator requires ~60-70 GPU hours on MetaWorld, and the metagradient estimator takes 3-4 days on 4 A100s for OXE. The authors admit datamodel estimation costs several times more than simply training on all data, which undercuts the practical value proposition of selection.

Real-world evaluations were conducted with a single seed, so the headline OXE gains (e.g., 61.0 vs. 40.0 average) have no statistical support; LIBERO margins are also small (37.76 vs. 36.4 for BR), with DataMIL losing to baselines on several individual tasks (e.g., Stove-Moka, Mug-Mug).

Several components appear hand-tuned per setting in ways that weaken the 'end-to-end, assumption-free' narrative: e.g., the pre-grasp state up-weighting (w=2) used only for LIBERO, different BC loss forms for different estimators, task-specific selection ratios (0.5%-1%), and different clustering granularities chosen per dataset.

The proxy metric's validity (validation loss as a stand-in for rollout success) is validated only on a handful of MetaWorld tasks (Fig. 2, Fig. 11); a more extensive correlation study between proxy metric and true success would strengthen the central claim.

The MetaWorld experiments use a simple state-based MLP while the hardest settings use Octo; the mismatch between the setting where the (expensive) regression estimator is validated and the settings where the metagradient estimator is used makes it harder to attribute gains to the proposed estimator choices.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: selecting useful data from large, heterogeneous prior robot datasets in an end-to-end, performance-aware manner, where existing heuristic (similarity-based) approaches demonstrably fall short.

Technically sound adaptation of the datamodels framework to robotics: the surrogate proxy metric (Eq. 5, negative BC loss on held-out target demos) is a sensible and well-argued solution to the non-differentiability and rollout-cost problems, and the paper validates it directly (Fig. 2, Fig. 11) against the true rollout metric, showing only a marginal drop.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, and real-world OXE selection (including the challenging cross-embodiment Tiago-Sink and multitask Droid settings), with strong quantitative gains (e.g., 10% average improvement over the best baseline on MetaWorld; 61.0 vs 40.0 real-world average).

Thoughtful engineering contributions that go beyond naive datamodel application: trajectory/sub-trajectory clustering to reduce influence-estimate noise, inclusion of target data to mitigate distribution shift, and the use of metagradient-based estimators to scale to large policies like Octo.

Good baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR, plus Target-Only and All-Data/Random controls), useful ablations (selection %, cluster size, co-training ratio, longer training for the All-Data baseline), and transparent analysis of what data is selected and why baselines fail.
Honest limitations section and a candid discussion of discrepancies with prior reported numbers (STRAP), including evaluation-protocol and architecture confounds; code and website promised.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core method is a careful transplantation of datamodels [13,16,35] into imitation learning, with the main novelty being the proxy metric and robotics-specific modifications (clustering, distribution-shift mitigation) rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Real-world evaluations use a single seed and modest rollout counts (e.g., 14-39 rollouts per task, ~50-60 datapoints in Table 1), so the OXE gains, while large, carry substantial statistical uncertainty.

LIBERO improvements are marginal on average (37.76 vs 36.4 for BR), and per-task results are mixed (e.g., Mug-Mug 0.8 vs 6.4 for Flow; Stove-Moka below STRAP), showing the method is not uniformly better even in a relatively benign setting.

The method has significant computational overhead (metagradient estimation is 3-5x slower than standard training; OXE selection takes 3-4 days on 4 A100s) and several sensitive hyperparameters (cluster size, selection ratio, co-training ratio, per-task proxy-loss weighting such as the hand-tuned w=2 for pre-grasp states) for which the paper acknowledges it lacks principled guidance.

The proxy metric's validity is established mainly in MetaWorld with a small policy; a systematic study of when validation BC loss is a reliable surrogate for success (e.g., for diffusion policies or under severe distribution shift) is limited to a few tasks.

In MetaWorld, the prior dataset contains expert demonstrations of the target tasks themselves, which makes the selection problem easier than the cross-task/cross-embodiment transfer emphasized elsewhere; the hardest claims rest on the fewest trials.
